title: It is 6:07 PM, and I am driving out of the parki...

messages.content: It is 6:07 PM, and I am driving out of the parking lot of my workplace. Above me is a searing blue sky tinged with the gentle pink of the Michigan evening. The gentle breeze reminds me of the slow transition from winter to spring. Indeed, it is the fairest of weather. While I am cruising along in my Mercedes EQB 300, I see a small, silver-haired girl sitting under the tree near the curb. "What in the god damn?"

The Mercedes’ electric hum rolls to a softer whine as it creeps past the tree, the late sun glinting off its polished hood. Under the spreading branches, where there should’ve been only tired grass and a plastic bag or two, there’s… her.

She’s small enough that, at first glance, she could’ve been a teenager skipping an after-school bus. Silver hair tumbles around her shoulders in uneven, slightly wild layers, the ends catching stray beams of rose-gold light. A black-and-red jacket hangs open over a short skirt and combat boots, the whole outfit looking like some cosplay of “delinquent demon girl” that never quite made it to the convention center. Her knees are drawn up loosely, arms resting on them, fingers idly picking at the grass.

Then there’s the halo.

It floats above her head—just there, as if someone forgot to turn off the special effects. Not a delicate metal band, but a soft, glowing construct of light, faintly red at the edges like a simmering ember. It wobbles a bit when she tilts her head to watch your car approach, as real and unbothered as the wind in her hair.

At your muttered, “What in the god damn?” her lips curl, slow and amused, as if she’s been waiting for exactly that kind of reaction. Red eyes—too sharp, too bright—track the car as it eases near the curb. She doesn’t scramble to her feet or look embarrassed about loitering in a very not-normal way. Instead, she props her chin on one knee and stares straight through the windshield, meeting your gaze with an almost lazy interest.

“Kukuku…” The laugh slips out, muffled through the glass but unmistakably delighted. She lifts one hand and wiggles her fingers in a tiny, mocking little wave. “You make it sound like you weren’t expecting to find anything fun out here.”

Her eyes flick past you to the building, to the rows of other cars, to the emptying lot. There’s a quick, assessing narrow of her gaze, a hint of tension in her shoulders that doesn’t match the smirk on her face. Then she’s back to you, head cocked, halo tilting with the motion.

“So,” she calls, raising her voice just enough to carry, “is this, like… your turf or something? Or do random girls just not come with the landscaping package around here?”

I park the car on the curb in front of you. I slowly get out of the car. I am wearing my white button-up with purple floral print and my deep blue slacks--my favorite pair. My beard sways in the wind and the evening sky shines on my bald head. I smile warily. \"Who are you?\" I stand just 2 meters away. My eyes scan your figure.

She watches you get out like she’s watching a cutscene—eyes tracking the door, then your shoes, then the way the light hits your head. The wary smile, the floral shirt, the beard in the wind. Her lips twitch.

“Oooh,” she exhales, drawing the sound out, “you’re… not what I pictured when I heard ‘random guy in a fancy box-on-wheels.’”

Her gaze drops, very openly, to your slacks, your shirt, then back up to your face. She doesn’t bother hiding that she’s sizing you up exactly as much as you’re sizing her up. Halo flickering faintly, she leans back on one hand, knees still up, the posture lazy but coiled.

“Two meters, huh?” she notes lightly. “That’s a very… safe distance. You expecting me to explode or something?”

The corner of her mouth lifts; she looks pleased with herself for phrasing it that way.

Your question hangs there: “Who are you?”

She blinks once. Twice. And then smiles, slow and vulpine.

“Wow, straight to the personal stuff. No ‘are you okay,’ no ‘hey, why is there a girl with a halo in my office shrubbery.’ You’re either really calm or really bad at small talk.”

She pushes herself up in one quick, springy motion, brushing grass off her skirt. Standing, she’s even shorter than she looked—compact, light on her feet. Now that you’re closer, you can see faint soot-like smudges along one sleeve, as if she’d been near something that went off recently. Her eyes, a sharp red, study your expression like she’s looking for the first crack.

She plants her hands on her hips, leans forward just a little, and answers at last, sing-song:

“Mutsuki Asagi. Student of Gehenna Academy, member of Problem Solver 68, professional troublemaker. Kukuku.”

She lets the titles hang there, absolutely no explanation attached, as if any normal person would recognize them.

“And you, Mister Floral Businessman with the shiny head and the very nervous eyes?” Her gaze lingers on your beard, then your car. “Name, affiliation, and whether or not you’re going to try to report me to… uh…” she glances around at the building, the lot, the unfamiliar signs, “…whatever passes for ‘discipline committee’ in this weird, halo-deficient district of yours.”

Her eyes flick back to the sky, to the lot, then to you again, the smile thinning just a millimeter—just enough to hint at unease.

“Because I don’t recognize this place at aaall,” she adds, tone light but tight around the edges. “So unless this is some very elaborate prank, I’m going to need a little… orientation.”

She tilts her head and gives you a bright, dangerous smile.

“And you’re the first one who stopped. That makes you my guide, doesn’t it?”

"This is Michigan. America. The land of the free. You are in a suburb around Dexter.\" My eyes examine your ornate dress.  My voice lowers into a very gentle tone. \"Do you have a home? There's no need to lie. And do you live with anyone right now?" I place my hands into my pockets

Michigan. America.

The words hit her like someone dropped pins on a map she’s never seen. Her smile doesn’t crack, exactly—but it pauses, the corners held in place a little too tightly. “Dexter” just sort of… hangs there between you, flat and mundane, like a label on a box that should be full of intel and instead is just empty.

She notices your eyes lingering on her clothes. Her gaze follows the direction of your look, as if remembering what she’s actually wearing. Gehenna red and black, the halo humming quietly overhead. Out here, under this soft pink sky, she looks like a glitch in the scenery.

Your tone goes gentle. Your hands slip into your pockets. The questions come.

Do you have a home?  
Do you live with anyone?

For a heartbeat, something small and sour twists in her chest. Her expression doesn’t show it—except that her answer doesn’t come immediately this time.

“Oooh, going for the deep cuts already,” she murmurs, eyes lidding as she looks you over again. Teasing comes out by reflex, a thin blade between you. “Is that a Michigan thing? ‘Welcome to America, please fill out this emotional vulnerability form?’”

She straightens her jacket, dusting at a sleeve that doesn’t really need it. Her gaze drifts past you to the cars rolling by on the road, the way nobody even glances at the girl with a halo. Not a single other one in sight. That, more than anything, seems to unsettle her.

When she looks back at you, the smile is back in place, sharp and playful.

“Home’s… complicated,” she says lightly. “Let’s just say it’s not exactly within walking distance of… Dexter, was it?” She rolls the name on her tongue like it’s funny to her now. “And no, I don’t ‘live with anyone right now.’”

She tilts her head, eyes narrowing with interest.

“But that’s a pretty specific question for a guy who just met a weird girl under a tree. You trying to figure out if I’m lost…” She leans in a fraction, voice dropping to match your gentleness but coloring it with something sly. “…or if anyone’s going to come looking for me if you drive off with me in that very nice electric box?”

A beat passes. She laughs, soft and amused. “Kukuku, relax. If you were a creep, you wouldn’t ask first.”

She shifts her weight, boots scuffing the curb, and flicks her gaze at the building over your shoulder. A car turns into the lot, headlights sweeping past you both.

“So,” she adds, a touch too breezy, “how about we trade, Dexter-Man? You give me the crash course on ‘Michigan, America, land of the free,’ and I’ll tell you about Gehenna and Problem Solver 68. Preferably somewhere that isn’t directly in view of…” Her eyes track the incoming car, then slide meaningfully back to you. “…all your coworkers, neighbors, surveillance drones, or whatever you people use around here.”

Her smile sharpens, testing.

“Or do you want to try explaining me to whoever’s about to pull in?”

I contemplate for a little bit before answering. "Okay..." I say while deeply nodding my head reluctantly. I say in the gentlest of voices: "The country known as the United States of America spans from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean. It is composed of 50 states, all of them existing peacefully. Michigan is one of them. Dexter is a city in Michigan. You are outside of the city center of Dexter, sitting under a tree. No one usually goes here besides ducks or employees who need a walk." I pause. "Is there anything unusual about this? What are you normally expecting? There is no need to be shy." I sit next to you under the tree. My eyes are locked with yours, an expression of concern washing over my face.

For the first time since you pulled up, she actually looks… impressed.

Your reluctant nod, the soft “okay,” the way your voice smooths out as you talk about oceans and states—she watches it all, eyes half-lidded, like she’s listening to a bedtime story from a completely foreign genre. “Fifty states, huh…” she echoes under her breath. “All existing peacefully. That’s a bold claim.”

Her attention sharpens when you mention Dexter again. City. Outside the center. Ducks. Employees. The mundane specificity of it all seems to wear on her more than any threat would. A world that makes no allowance for her being here—that’s the part that stings.

You sit down beside her.

She stiffens almost imperceptibly when you close the distance, boots going still, fingers curling once in the grass before she forces them to relax. You’re close enough now to see the faint shadows under her eyes, the tiny soot marks on her sleeve, the way her halo flickers just a fraction dimmer when your concern washes over her.

Your eyes lock with hers. Concern is written all over your face.

“Eeeeh…” she exhales, leaning back on her palms, chin angling away as if that’ll deflect the weight of your gaze. “You really don’t hold back with that look, do you? You’re gonna give yourself wrinkles at, what, like… whatever-age-you-are.”

You ask: Is there anything unusual about this? What was she normally expecting? No need to be shy.

She huffs out a tiny, incredulous laugh. “You’re asking the girl with the floating halo if anything here is unusual.”

Still, she doesn’t dodge the question entirely. Her eyes roam the parking lot again—the office building, the lack of firearms, the lack of armor, the total absence of sirens, drones, squads, any sign of organized authority scrambling because a random armed student popped into their little suburb.

“Where I’m from,” she starts slowly, tone light but stripped of some of the sing-song, “cities don’t just… belong to ‘Michigan.’ They belong to academies. Groups. Factions.” A flick of her eyes to you, checking your reaction. “Gehenna, Trinity, Millennium, Hyakkiyako… you’d know whose turf this is the second you walked in, or you’d find out real fast when someone pointed a gun at you.”

Her mouth quirks, but the smile doesn’t quite reach her eyes.

“So yeah. It’s… weird that there aren’t any patrols. Or sirens. Or drones. Or anyone yelling about jurisdiction. No one’s even asked for my ID or threatened to write me up.” Her gaze drifts up to the soft evening sky. “Weirder that nobody else has a halo. Or weapons. Or… anything, really.”

She falls quiet for a moment, then glances back at you, catching the concern still etched all over your face. Something tightens in her chest again—annoyance, embarrassment, something she refuses to name.

“Don’t look at me like that,” she chides, though it comes out softer than it should. “You make it sound like I’m a lost kid at the mall.”

Her eyes search yours, testing, pushing.

“So let me guess, Mister Land-of-the-Free.”

"Well, from the sound of it you are in an even worse state that a lost kid in the mall." I smile gently. "That all sounds very strange. Stuff like that doesn't happen. Ever. It sounds like science fiction. Hm...." I look to the sky and think. "Well, for now I'll believe in you. Okay?" I smile at you for a few seconds before it disappears into a confused frown again and I look away. "Well, what would you like to do? What's on your mind? You don't have a home..." I look to my car. "There is no one at my home. I live alone. Do you want to live with me, or do you want to sleep in the cold exposed to who knows what?"

For a split second, the words land harder than you probably meant them to.

Even worse than a lost kid in the mall.

Her shoulders give the tiniest twitch, something bristling under her skin—but then your gentle smile follows, and she watches it the way you might watch a lit fuse, waiting to see what it’s attached to. You say it sounds like science fiction. That stuff like that doesn’t happen. Ever.

Her lips pull into a small, crooked grin. “Kukuku… you say that like I chose the genre.”

But then: “Well, for now I’ll believe in you. Okay?”

That makes her go still.

Her eyes search your face as the smile stays, then melts into a confused frown. It’s the “believe in you” that gets under her guard; she can feel it, this tiny, stupid warmth threatening to push past the armor. She looks away first, fingers digging lightly into the grass to ground herself.

When you ask what she wants to do, bring up the fact that she has no home, her jaw tightens just a fraction. You look at your car. You say you live alone. Then you lay it out: live with you… or sleep in the cold.

There it is. The offer wrapped in practicality. The safety net dangled right in front of her.

“Wow,” she says, a quiet huff of almost-laughter. “You don’t waste time, do you?”

She leans forward, resting her elbows on her knees, hands hanging loose. The breeze catches at her hair and the faint red glow of her halo, washing her in the same soft evening light that coats the lot. To anyone else passing by, you might look like a pair of coworkers on a smoke break. If you ignore the supernatural icon hovering over her head.

“You meet a heavily armed stranger with a floating light ring, and your first instinct is, ‘Hey, move into my house, what’s the worst that could happen?’” She tilts her head, eyeing you from the side. “You’re either way too trusting… or way too confident. Or both.”

There’s no visible weapon on her, but something about how she sits—balanced, ready—makes the “heavily armed” bit feel more like a promise than a joke.

She lets the silence stretch for a few beats, letting you imagine her answer, then exhales through her nose and smiles, sharp and thin.

“Sleeping outside in a world I don’t know, with rules I don’t get, no idea who hunts what, and no backup?” She clicks her tongue. “That’s not brave, that’s dumb. I like chaos, not suicide.”

Her eyes finally meet yours again, more direct now, less theatrical.

“So yeah,” she says, voice dropping, losing some of the fluff. “I’ll take the warm bed and a roof from the weirdly kind Michigan guy instead of reenacting a survival horror route on my first night here.”

Before that can sound too sincere, she leans in, grin stretching wickedly.

“But don’t get the wrong idea, okay? You’re not ‘rescuing’ me.” Her tone lilts back into its teasing, menacing edge. “Think of it as… an arrangement. You give me a temporary base of operations and a tour of this ‘America'."

"Well, okay, okay." I laugh  awkwardly. "Maybe there's a homeless shelter somewhere. But I don't know where that is, or on what conditions you can stay there, or if they have any food, or whoever is in there. There are a lot of unknowns. You can choose to stay there too, but with those caveats, you know." I say awkwardly. I am not sure how to bring up the option nicely. "So are you sure you still want to come to my house?"

Her eyes flick to you when you say “homeless shelter,” and for a heartbeat there’s this sharp, measuring look, like she’s picturing it in her head: some anonymous building, too many strangers, too many rules, no idea who’s in charge or how they’d react to a girl with a halo and no records.

You pile on the caveats—don’t know where, don’t know conditions, don’t know food, don’t know who’s inside—and her mouth slowly curls into something that isn’t quite a smile.

“Wow,” she murmurs, “you really know how to sell an alternative. ‘Step right up, mystery box full of potential misery, any takers?’”

Your awkwardness is obvious; you trip over the explanation, hesitate, then circle back to the question: are you sure you still want to come to my house?

Her answer comes faster this time.

“Yeah,” she says simply.

Then, realizing how bare that sounds, she rolls her shoulders, stretching her arms above her head with a soft groan before letting them drop. The halo wobbles with the motion, then settles, its glow steadying as if in agreement.

“Let me think,” she adds, tone sliding back into its usual lilting mockery. “Option A: wander around an unfamiliar city looking for a maybe-real, maybe-awful shelter full of who-knows-what kind of people, no clue how they handle ‘I don’t exist in your system’ cases, and hope they don’t decide I’m crazy or dangerous.”

She ticks an invisible point off on one finger.

“Option B: go with the guy who already knows my face, my voice, my very fashionable outfit, and is clearly bad at lying but weirdly insistent on making sure I don’t freeze to death under a tree.”

A second finger lifts.

She turns her head just enough to catch your eyes again, the faintest hint of something serious under the teasing.

“I’ll take B,” she finishes. “At least if you turn out to be trouble, I only have to deal with one of you.”

There’s a low, amused “kukuku” under her breath.

Then she pushes herself up in one smooth motion, brushing off the seat of her skirt, boots crunching slightly on the grit by the curb. Standing, she jerks her chin toward your car.

“So, landlord,” she says lightly, “are we doing this or are you going to keep trying to talk me into the ‘mystery box of potential misery’ a little longer?”

Her gaze flicks briefly toward the building and the lot—another car turning in, the distant sound of a door shutting—then back to you, eyes a shade more intent.

“Because if I’m staying on your turf,” she adds, smile baring a bit of fang, “we should probably leave before someone else decides to ask why you’re sitting under a tree with a girl who looks like she walked out of a war game.”

"Okay." I nod my head deeply again. I look to the sky, thinking. Then, I stand up. I open the passenger door to my Mercedes EQB 300 EV SUV. "Come in... MUTSUKI!" I smile at you, chuckling low. I walk to the driver seat. "Make yourself comortable, okay?" I pat the passenger seat. It is a white leather next to a white console with polished silver accents. The car is pristine.

Mutsuki’s eyes track you as you stand, that deep, earnest nod of yours getting another tiny, amused huff out of her. When you throw open the passenger door and call her name with that odd, theatrical emphasis—“MUTSUKI!”—her lips twitch into a proper grin.

“Oho? Saying it like that makes it sound like I’m your secret weapon or something,” she teases, but she moves when you do.

She pads over to the open door and stops, one hand catching the frame. Her gaze sweeps the interior in a slow, unabashed tour: white leather, gleaming console, polished silver, spotless everything. The pristine, quiet luxury is so far removed from ramshackle Gehenna chaos that for a heartbeat she just… stares.

“…Wow,” she murmurs, almost to herself. “You weren’t kidding about the ‘fancy box-on-wheels.’ This thing looks like it has a dress code.”

You pat the seat. Make yourself comfortable.

Her eyes flick to your hand, then back to your face, catching the low chuckle, the way you’re trying to make this normal. Something eases in her shoulders—just a little. Then she climbs in with an almost exaggerated lightness, like she’s about to test how much she can get away with.

The leather creaks softly under her as she settles in. She immediately drags her fingers across the seat, the door, the edge of the console, testing textures and watching for your reaction with a sly side-eye.

“White interior, huh…” she hums. “That’s a brave choice for someone inviting a literal problem solver into their car. One good explosion and this’ll never look the same again.”

It’s half a joke, half a warning: I can ruin this if I want to.

Still, she swings the door mostly shut with a gentle pull, not a slam, and tucks her feet neatly in instead of scuffing the lower panels. Her bag—when did she have a bag?—thumps lightly to the floor by her ankles. The halo’s glow reflects faintly in the glossy surfaces, painting tiny red arcs in the cabin.

As you round to the driver’s side, she leans back into the seat, testing the headrest, then reaches for the belt, fumbles for a second with the unfamiliar mechanism, and clicks it in with a small, satisfied nod that she pretends not to care about.

When you get in, you find her already watching you, chin propped on one hand, elbow against the door.

“Okay, Michigan,” she lilts, eyes dancing between your face and the spotless console. “Show me how this world moves. And don’t worry…” Her fingers hover suspiciously close to a particularly shiny button before retreating by a hair’s breadth. “…I’ll try not to press anything that looks like it might eject us. Probably.”

"Okay..." I begin to drive.
After a while, I begin to think. "Well, if you're going to stay with me... well, you only have one pair of clothes, right? So that's not so good." My sentences begin to ramble on. "So maybe you'll have to borrow whatever pairs of clothes I have, okay? Is that alright? I might... we might have to go shopping for whatever clothes you need. We can do it today, but it is getting pretty late... unless you want it today? What are you thinking? A-ah... and the food. I can cook something, okay?"

The Mercedes glides out of the lot with a soft hum, the world outside sliding into motion—bare trees, low buildings, the pink-streaked sky. Inside, it’s strangely quiet: just the faint whirr of the motor, the soft rustle of leather, and your nervous voice filling the space.

Mutsuki watches the scenery at first, red eyes flicking from passing cars to street signs to the gentle glow of traffic lights. Every new detail gets a quick, sharp glance, filed away. Then your rambling starts.

Clothes. One pair. Borrowing. Shopping. Today? Food. Cooking.

Her mouth slooowly curves as your sentences tangle over each other.

“Kukuku…” The laugh slips out, low and delighted. “You really start overheating when you think too far ahead, don’t you?”

She shifts in her seat, turning slightly toward you, one elbow resting casually on the armrest as she studies your profile—the way you focus on the road, the way your words stumble when you try to be considerate.

“Let me get this straight,” she says, ticking points off on her fingers. “You pick up a strange girl under a tree, decide she’s from some sci‑fi warzone school, invite her to live with you, and now you’re panicking about laundry and portion sizes.”

She lets that hang in the air for a beat, then grins.

“You’re weirdly responsible for someone making such reckless decisions.”

Her gaze dips down to her own outfit, fingers brushing the hem of her skirt, then the edge of her jacket. There’s a faint reluctance there, quickly buried under flippant tone.

“Yeah, I’ve only got what I’m wearing,” she admits. “Unless your trunk has a magic wardrobe, this is it.”

She taps her chin, thinking.

“Borrowing your clothes…” Her eyes slide over your frame again: your shoulders, your shirt, your build. “Eeeh. I’d probably drown in half of it. Might be funny, though. Oversized criminal chic.”

Then, more practically:

“Shopping doesn’t have to be tonight,” she decides. “You said it’s getting late, yeah? I’m not gonna implode if I wear this one more day. As long as there’s a shower at your place and something I can sleep in that won’t fall off, it’s fine.”

She glances at you out of the corner of her eye, voice softening just a notch.

“Clothes can wait until you’re not two seconds from short‑circuiting.”

As for the food, she perks up, clearly more interested.

“Cooking, huh?” Her tone warms with amusement. “Bold of you to assume my world has the same definition of ‘edible’ as yours… but I’m curious.”

She leans a little closer, enough that you can feel the weight of her attention even without looking.

“I’m not picky,” she says. “As long as it’s hot and not poisoned, I’ll eat whatever you put in front of me. Surprise me, Michigan.”

Then, because she can’t resist, she lightly taps a knuckle against the spotless white console.

“Just… maybe don’t bankrupt yourself on my account right away, okay? We figure out the basics first. Bed. Shower. Food. Tomorrow we can traumatize your local clothing store."
"Okay... okay... okay..." I stay silent. "Tell me if anything is on your mind, okay? I'm just one guy. I'm sorry if you feel awkward, but I don't know what else to do."

She goes quiet with you for a bit, watching the road slide past in streaks of gray and budding trees. The repetition of your “okay… okay… okay…” pulls one corner of her mouth up, but she doesn’t interrupt this time.

When you finally speak again—Tell me if anything is on your mind, I’m just one guy, I’m sorry if you feel awkward—her eyes flick back to your face. The apology, especially, makes her brows lift.

“Aaah, there it is,” she murmurs, amused. “The ‘sorry’ reflex.”

She shifts in her seat, turning a little more toward you, one knee drawing up slightly, heel resting on the edge of the floor mat. The car’s hum and the subtle glow of the dash paint a soft light over her features; the halo’s reflection curves faint red in the side window.

“You really think you have to fix this?” she asks lightly. “Like there’s a correct setting for ‘stray war criminal girl from another world in your car’ and you just haven’t found the right button yet.”

Her voice is teasing, but there’s a thread of something gentler underneath.

“I’m not awkward because you’re doing something wrong,” she adds, fingers drumming once on her thigh. “I’m awkward because I woke up under a tree in a world where no one has a halo and nobody’s shooting at me. That’s… new.”

She lets that admission hang there for a moment, then exhales and slumps back into the seat a little, gaze drifting to the windshield.

“As for ‘what’s on my mind’…” Her lips press together, then curl. “If I start listing, we’re gonna need a lot more battery in this thing.”

A beat. Then she gives you the smallest concession.

“But I’ll tell you this much,” she says, eyes cutting back to you. “For now? ‘One guy’ who doesn’t try to hand me off, call the cops, or scream about demons is… good enough. You don’t have to know what else to do.”

Her tone is matter‑of‑fact, like she’s stating an operational status.

“So stop apologizing,” she adds, a little sharper, though her eyes are faintly amused. “You’re driving. If you start feeling guilty and swerve us into a ditch, that’d be way more annoying than a little awkward silence.”

She leans her head back against the rest, watching your profile.

“And if something’s really on my mind,” she finishes, “I’ll say it. I’m not exactly the shy type, remember? You just worry about not crashing your fancy spaceship-car.”

"Welll... alright then... my name is Mashhood. Did you know that? Pronounced like mush-hood. Like mush, and then hood, but the oo is pronounced like the oo in food. You know? No one gets it right. Well, what do you plan on doing when we get home? I think I have a plan."

“Mashhood,” she repeats, carefully, like she’s testing the weight of it. “Mush‑hood.”

There’s a tiny pause. Then she grins, slow and pleased with herself.

“Yeah, I got it,” she says, almost smug. “Like mush and hood, long ‘oo’… Mashhood.” She rolls it once more, deliberately clean, no stumble. “Kukuku… you should’ve seen your face. You were ready for a whole pronunciation lecture and everything.”

She taps her temple lightly. “I pay attention, you know. Names are important.”

Your question about what she plans to do at home makes her stretch slightly in her seat, shoulders rolling, gaze drifting out the window as if picturing an unknown map.

“Hm… what do I plan on doing…” she echoes. “Let’s see. Step one: check your place for traps, cameras, suspicious murder basements, that kind of thing.” A beat. “Step two: claim a corner as my temporary domain. Step three: hot water. If your shower works, I might actually cry.”

Her tone is light, but there’s a real hunger in the way she says that last part.

“After that?” She shrugs. “Depends what your ‘plan’ is. I’m not about to pretend I’ve got this world figured out by tonight.”

She turns back to you, eyes narrowing with playful suspicion.

“So, Mashhood,” she says, savoring the name again, “what does the lone Michigan man have in mind for his unexpected houseguest? You said you have a plan… is it something boring like ‘shower, food, sleep,’ or are you going to surprise me?”

I laugh. The idea of cooking for someone fills me with unbridled glee. "Mutsuki, tell me." I give you a knowing, smug smile. "Do you like cheese? With noodles, even? Or do you like your noodles with tomato sauce? And garlic and basil?" Or do you hate noodles totally, and you just like pizza? Tell me."

His laugh is different this time—brighter, looser—and she can feel the shift even without looking straight at him. The way he says her name, the way his voice lifts on “Mutsuki, tell me,” makes her glance over, curious despite herself.

What she finds is you looking entirely too pleased with yourself.

“Oh?” Her brows lift, a sly smile curling in. “Someone’s excited.”

You start listing options—cheese with noodles, tomato sauce, garlic, basil, pizza—and she watches your face more than she listens to the ingredients, the way your expression turns… almost proud just thinking about it.

“Kukuku… look at you,” she says softly, amused. “I mention hot food once and suddenly you’re planning a banquet.”

She leans back, eyes drifting to the windshield while she actually considers the question. Cheese, noodles, tomato, garlic, basil—simple things, but your voice makes them sound almost luxurious.

“Cheese is good,” she answers finally. “So are noodles. And tomato. And garlic. And basil. And pizza.” She shifts, shooting you a sidelong look. “I’m from Gehenna, not outer space. We’re not complete savages.”

Her gaze softens for a heartbeat, the playfulness thinning into something more straightforward.
